findings.text: the head arm's first line reads `revision: 51f2d62de0c14d9bcf8da7ce0d956dd3d4dd0289` — the base, not the head the arm is cited as evidence for. The arm ran at 12:44:44, 71 s before the node committed 34df161cb at 12:45:55, so at run time `git rev-parse HEAD` in that worktree genuinely was the base and the measured content existed only as uncommitted modifications of it. After the commit the two logs carry the same revision string, so the one field the node's fence singles out (`revision: <full sha>` on each) no longer distinguishes the arms, and a reader comparing them would conclude the same revision was measured twice — which the 84-versus-89 pass counts contradict. The tree, module and cwd lines do name the worktree, the worktree is clean at 34df161cb, and I reproduced both arms to the id, so the measurement is recoverable; what the header cannot do is tie the 89-passed arm to the commit it is offered for.

`_real_settings()` resolves the guard target through `getpwuid(os.getuid()).pw_dir`, while the file the command would actually write is `Path("~/.claude/settings.json").expanduser()` (reckon/hooks/install.py:134-136), which follows `HOME`. Set `HOME` elsewhere — as the node's own negative-control note says its run did, "home directory isolated" — and the four guarding cases fingerprint a file the command would never touch, so the guard passes while a write it exists to catch lands wherever `HOME` points. The guard is sound only under an unredirected `HOME`, an assumption nothing in the file states.

the replaced paragraph told the reader to drive the installer "run from the checkout root"; the replacement names the command and drops the directory, while the mechanism it protects is unchanged. A dry run I ran in the reviewed worktree printed commands beginning `<worktree>/.venv/bin/python <worktree>/reckon/hooks/...`, so an install performed from a worker worktree — where agents are told to run their commands — writes the operator's `~/.claude/settings.json` with hook commands naming a tree that is expected to be reclaimed, and the hook then fails the way the paragraph above it describes (silent, no user-visible symptom). The surviving sentence "always names the scripts of the checkout that composed it" states the mechanism but is not the instruction the removed clause was.

`hooks_install(scope, write, settings_path)` never reads `scope`; the target comes from `--settings` or from `install_hook_settings`'s own default. `click.Choice(["user"])` has one member, so no behaviour differs today, but the option advertises a selection it does not make: it is the entire surface by which the plan's `--scope user` is met and it is inert, so a scope added later would be accepted and silently ignored rather than redirected, and the reader who follows `--help` will believe the flag chose the file.

the fence and the evidence fragment both state that every case points the settings path at a temporary directory and compares the real user-scope settings file before and after. `test_install_help_lists_the_command` (tests/test_hooks_install_cli.py:60-66) does neither: it passes no `--settings` and never calls `_fingerprint`. Four of the five cases guard the real file and the fifth runs `--help`, which opens nothing, so no risk follows — but the sentence is false as written, which is the shape the node's own contract names (a check that reads as covering more than it does).

justifications.durability: the declared mutation reddens the case it names and does so with the declared string on the log's first line; the dry-run case asserts the target's bytes and the real file's mtime_ns-plus-bytes, so a same-bytes write would still red it; the duplicate case asserts the file is exactly as the first install left it; and the tests point every write at a temporary directory, which I confirmed by fingerprinting the real settings file across my own runs. justifications.evidence: both arms reproduced exactly under my own hand with identical failure ids, the five-test delta between them (84 to 89) is accounted for by a file that provably does not exist at the base revision, the CLI's three behaviours were driven directly rather than inferred from the suite, and the negative control is verbatim and red on the right case, which I re-ran myself in a scratch tree against the mutation the log names. Deducted for the head arm's revision line naming the base (finding 1), which is the one instrument the node's own fence relied on to bind each arm to a revision, and for the evidence sentence over-claiming its guard coverage (finding 5).
justifications.fit: wraps install_hook_settings instead of reimplementing, keeps the lazy import style of the surrounding CLI module, translates the installer's error into the click idiom, and adds one option (`--settings`) that the fence did not ask for but which is what makes the command testable without touching the operator's file. Deducted for `--scope`, an option that carries the plan's required spelling but selects nothing (finding 4), and for the refusal message being composed at the CLI from `result.skipped` rather than reusing a single installer-side phrasing.
justifications.goal_fidelity: the command is exactly the surface the goal names and behaves as the goal states when driven directly. The retention is the refusal's granularity: the fence's own sentence says any already-present entry refuses, and the code refuses only a whole-fragment duplicate. That reading is the one the plan's revision note supersedes and the one the installer's per-event skip forces, and the node recorded the mismatch for adjudication rather than resolving it silently, so it costs the score little.
justifications.scope_discipline: every changed path is inside the grant, the commit touches nothing else, no terminal status set, `landing:` written rather than a plan edit, and no figure written for a node whose done-when names no artifact. Byte-identical to what a reference-following worker owes.
